cat > docs/design.md <<'ENDOFPART'
# Two-way sync of customer and contact records

**Design document — Tequity Round 1**

Sales edits customers and contacts in Salesforce; finance and customer-success
edit the same records in the portal Tequity built on Postgres. Both copies must
agree within 30 seconds while both are up, every field's history must be kept,
and we control only our side.

This document is the decisions and the numbers. Parts 7–10 are the four rules
and all arithmetic is one table in 10.4; the argument behind each rule is in
[`design-appendix.md`](design-appendix.md), section by section, together with
the brief's scenario traced (**A**), the hardest race traced (**B**),
interfaces, schema DDL and sequences (**C**), each assumption derived with what
changes if it is wrong (**D**), and what the demo substitutes for (**E**).
`docs/adr/` has the three decisions expensive to reverse.

---

## Summary

The unit of sync is a **field**, not a record. Each field carries an **order
key** `(occurred_at, origin_rank, origin_event_id)`; the current value is the
one whose key is greatest.

**Salesforce has no merge logic** — it overwrites with whatever lands last. We
are the only party that compares anything, so our database holds the decision
and Salesforce's copy is a projection of it. Hence the one rule everything
follows from:

> **Outbound work is created exactly when `sf_value` — what we believe
> Salesforce holds for a field — differs from that field's current value.**
> Checked after every field, on both paths, nowhere else.
> *We call Salesforce when, and only when, we believe Salesforce disagrees with us.*

| Rule | | § |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Duplicate** | `eventId` claimed in the apply's own transaction; and the compare is strictly `>`, so a duplicate escaping the table is a no-op anyway | 8.1 |
| **Out of order** | order keys compared per field; a change not strictly newer never becomes current, and is kept as `superseded` with its actor and time | 8.2 |
| **Loop** | an echo makes `sf_value` equal the current value, so the condition goes false — no fuel after one hop | 9 |
| **6-h outage** | queue rows commit with the edit, so they survive a restart; on recovery the inbound sweep runs **before** the outbound drain | 10.3 |

**Numbers.** Peak 20 edits/s assumed, business-hours average 3, quiet hour 0.5.
We run at **70 of the 100 req/s** allowed, 11% used in steady state. A 6-hour
outage queues **19,440 changes → 14,954 calls**, draining in 5.1 min; with the
1.2-min sweep first, **6.3 min** (row 1, 10.4). The 30-second target closes at
~6 s both ways, 7 of the 9.8 worst-case seconds being Salesforce's.

---

## 1. Assumptions, and the questions I would ask

Nothing below was given. **Appendix D derives each one and says what changes if
it goes the other way.** The five the exercise names are A1, A3, A4, A7, A9;
**A4 and A5 assume Salesforce APIs the brief does not mention.**

| | Assumption |
| --- | --- |
| **A1** | **Peak 20 edits/s, business-hours average 3/s, quiet hour 0.5/s** (5 M records × ~4 touches/yr, 250-day 8-hour year, × 7 for peak). **10.4 uses the average; 10.1 says why** |
| **A2** | 70% of edits originate in Salesforce, 30% in the portal |
| **A3** | **A webhook carries only the changed fields**, per the sample |
| **A4** | **Salesforce can be queried for records changed in a window** — SOQL on `SystemModstamp`, 2,000 records/request. **Assumed, not given** |
| **A5** | **Creates can be made idempotent** by external-id upsert on our `portalId`. **Assumed, not given** |
| **A6** | `changedBy` names the API caller, so our integration user is recognisable in it |
| **A7** | **Delivery is at-least-once**; HTTPS, HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, retried on 5xx or timeout |
| **A8** | Throttling arrives as 429 or `REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, with `Retry-After` when available |
| **A9** | **On a portal save the time is our `clock_timestamp()` and the actor is the authenticated session** — never the body's `editedBy`, which a caller could forge |
| **A10** | Clock skew between the two clocks is at most 2 s |
| **A11** | `occurredAt` is UTC, millisecond resolution; two edits can share a millisecond |
| **A12** | The 100 req/s cap is ours alone to spend, and **we run at 70** |
| **A13** | Salesforce emits a webhook within 5 s p99; a record write returns within 2 s p99 |
| **A14** | The nine named fields are the whole schema |
| **A15** | No record is ever deleted (the exercise's scope) |
| **A16** | **The outage is dark both ways at once** — the brief's two sentences jointly imply it, and it is the harder reading |

**Questions I could not close with an assumption.**

1. **How is the webhook produced** — Apex callout, Platform Event, Change Data
   Capture, middleware? Decides A4, A6 and A11 together. Highest-value question.
2. **Is there an external-id field on Account and Contact we may write?** (A5.)
3. **What else in the client's org spends the API limit?** (A12; row 5, 10.4.)
4. **When two portal users edit one field, what should the second see?** 7.5 is
   my rule, but the choice is a product decision.
5. **Must history be retained legally, and does that conflict with
   right-to-erasure?** Part 4 never deletes a change.
6. **Is any field single-owner?** I assume not; if some are, part 7 simplifies
   for them and we need a per-field ownership table.

---

## 2. The systems, who calls whom, the network seam, the interfaces

```
 sales user                  finance / customer-success user
     | edits in                          | edits in
     v                                   v
+--------------+             +--------------------+
|  SALESFORCE  |             |  TEQUITY PORTAL    |
| their CRM+DB |             |  our app           |
+--------------+             +--------------------+
   |      ^                         | in-process
   |      |                         v
   |      |     +-------------------------------------+
   |      |     | MERGE  order keys, history, echo    |
   |      |     |        and repair decisions         |
   |      |     +-------------------------------------+
   |      |            |                     ^
   |      |            v                     |
   |      |     +-------------------------------------+
   |      |     | POSTGRES  records, field history,   |
   |      |     |           outbound queue            |
   |      |     +-------------------------------------+
   |      |           ^                       |
   | == PUBLIC INTERNET == the only path      v
   |      | (A) SF->us                 +-----------------+
   |      |      HTTPS webhook         | SYNC WORKER     |
   +------|------------> [EP] ---------| governor,       |
          | (B) us->SF                 | retries, sweep  |
          +----------------------------+-----------------+
            HTTPS record API: create / update / changed-since

 [EP] WEBHOOK ENDPOINT (ours): validate, dedupe, MERGE, commit, 200.
```

| Path | Caller | Callee | Trigger | Cap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | Salesforce | our webhook endpoint | a record changed in Salesforce | none — inbound is outside the cap |
| **B** | our sync worker | Salesforce record API | we believe Salesforce disagrees with us | 100 req/s hard; we run at 70 |
| — | the portal's save handler | MERGE, in-process | a portal user saved | not a network call |

No human crosses the internet seam; only paths A and B do.

**Two processes, one repository, and the seam between them is Postgres** — not
HTTP, not a broker ([ADR 0001](adr/0001-two-processes-with-postgres-as-the-seam.md)).
The endpoint must never block on Salesforce, and the worker is the single
governor of a shared cap. In one database the inbound apply and the outbound
enqueue are **one commit**, so "we changed a value" and "we owe Salesforce a
call" cannot disagree after a crash.

| Crosses the boundary | Written by | Read by | Means |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `outbound_change` | endpoint and portal, in the merge transaction | sync worker | "we believe Salesforce disagrees about this field" |
| `echo_fence` | sync worker, after a successful send | endpoint | "we just wrote this value; expect it back" |

**The interface on each side is Appendix C.1**: our endpoint's contract and
status codes, the three Salesforce operations we depend on — each idempotent **by
design**, which is what makes at-least-once sending safe — and `applyChanges`,
the one interface every edit path goes through. **A 200 is returned only after
our transaction commits.**

**Does 30 seconds close?** Yes, at ~6 s both ways:

| Portal → Salesforce | p99 | Salesforce → portal | p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| commit (queue row is in it) | — | Salesforce emits (A13, **not ours**) | 5.0 s |
| worker notices (`NOTIFY`, 1 s poll fallback) | 1.0 s | network | 0.5 s |
| coalescing window | 1.0 s | our apply transaction | 0.2 s |
| queue wait at 11% utilisation | 0.1 s | | |
| Salesforce write (A13, **not ours**) | 2.0 s | | |
| **total** | **4.1 s** | **total** | **5.7 s** |

**No inbound queue** — at A1's peak the endpoint commits 14 transactions a
second.

---

## 3. The subproblems, in the order I would build them

**Ordered by risk:** (1) getting it wrong loses data unrecoverably, (2) getting
it wrong is silent, (3) other code is built on the decision. That puts the merge
rule first and the backfill last — the opposite of the data's flow.

| | Subproblem | Why here | Demo |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **S1** | decide a field's current value, and keep what it displaced | all three: a wrong merge loses a real edit permanently and silently, and every write path is built on its schema | **yes** |
| **S2** | stop a change going round forever | the only self-amplifying failure — a loop eats the whole cap and stops sync for every record | **yes** |
| **S3** | hold outbound work on disk and spend the cap | S1's severity at lower likelihood; a transactional outbox is a known shape | **yes** |
| **S4** | make inbound delivery safe to repeat and to reorder | cannot be earlier ("older" needs S1's key); severe but detectable and replayable | **yes** |
| **S5** | know which record is which across the systems | a lost create response can duplicate a record: bad, but bounded and visible at once | no |
| **S6** | recover what was missed while a side was dark | **first to ask about**, sixth to build: fixed by re-running, but rests on A4 | no |
| **S7** | prove the webhook came from Salesforce | a gate, not a risk; stubbed day one, filled before production | no |
| **S8** | load the 5 million existing records | one-off, offline, no latency target, re-runnable | no |

**The demo exercises S1–S4 and nothing below** — exactly the four whose failures
are unrecoverable or silent: phone-and-city with full history (S1), our own
update returning and not being sent back (S2), a pending call surviving a restart
with Salesforce down and then draining under an enforced cap (S3), a duplicate
and an older event after a newer one (S4). S2, S6, S7 and S8 add **no process**.

---

## 4. The data we store

Eight tables; Appendix C.2 has the DDL.
[ADR 0002](adr/0002-merge-per-field-not-per-record.md): **the unit of sync is a
field** — forced, since the brief's scenario has a portal city edit and a
Salesforce phone edit concurrent with each other, and a record-level comparison
must discard one, unable to see they touched different fields.

| Table | Holds | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `customer`, `contact` | **the current values**, typed | they live **here and nowhere else** |
| `field_version` | the **order key** per `(record, field)`, plus `sf_value` / `sf_observed_at` — what we believe Salesforce holds. Moved by a Salesforce observation **and by our own successful send** | a **cache, not a second truth**; also the row MERGE locks |
| `field_change` | **the history**: append-only, `applied` and `superseded`, both **permanent** | what the client is buying; `superseded` stays because the brief says an earlier edit stays on record |
| `sync_observation` | `echo`, `confirmed`, `restatement`; 90-day partitions | not edits by people, so not history |
| `inbound_event` | the duplicate key, 30-day retention (104 MB) | 8.1 |
| `outbound_change` | the **durable queue** — which field is owed, **never the value** | 6.3 |
| `record_link` | Salesforce id ↔ portal id, and the per-record lock | a portal-created record has a `portal_id` first |
| `echo_fence`, `sync_watermark` | "we just wrote this" (15-min TTL); how far through Salesforce's history we are sure | 9, 10.3 |

**Does the storage close?** 5 M typed rows at 1.2 GB; **27 M** `field_version`
rows (1 M × 3 fields + 4 M × 6) at 5.5 GB with its index; `field_change` at
**26 M rows/year** (20 M edits × 1.3 fields) and **5.2 GB/yr, kept forever
because it is the product**. **~13 GB in year one, growing 5 GB/yr.**

---

## 5. The inbound path

**One HTTP request becomes one Postgres transaction**, with no network call
inside it and no background step. The sequence is Appendix C.3: validate, claim
the `eventId`, lock the record, then per field **(a) learn → (b) restatement →
(c) decide → (d) repair**, then commit and answer 200.

- **(a) learn** records what Salesforce holds regardless of what (c) decides,
  which is what collapses repair into the single condition 8.3.
- **(b) restatement** skips a field restating the `sf_value` we already held
  (8.4).
- **(c) decide** takes the first case that applies — echo, then
  value-already-equal (`confirmed`), then the order-key comparison, then
  `superseded` — and only here can a current value change.
- **(d) repair** is condition 8.3, after every field whatever happened to it.

Three properties are deliberate. **The duplicate claim and the apply share one
transaction** — split them and a crash between marks an event processed that was
never applied, which Salesforce will never resend (A7 promises redelivery only
until we answer 200). **No network call is inside it**, keeping the endpoint's
p99 at 200 ms. **Fields are independent** — one event may apply `phone` and
supersede `city`, and the event's own outcome is then `partial`.

> A change whose canonical value already equals the current value changes
> **nothing** — not the value, not the order key, and not history.

| Resolving the record | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** known `sf_id` | one indexed lookup, lock, proceed |
| **(b)** unknown `sf_id`, `changedBy` a human | a Salesforce-created record we have not seen: mint a `portal_id`, insert the link and an empty row, apply every field as a first write. **Recovery (10.3) reuses this path** |
| **(c)** unknown `sf_id`, `changedBy` the integration user | the echo of a create *we* made, arriving before we recorded the id it returned. **Answer 503 + `Retry-After: 5`, apply nothing** — by the redelivery it is case (a). Bounded: after 60 s log loudly and treat as (b) |

**400 versus 500**, since a 400 discards the event forever: an unknown *field
name* earns one; a *value* we failed to canonicalise is our bug and earns a 500.

---

## 6. The outbound path

### 6.1 The portal save

The handler takes the same record lock as part 5, stamps `occurred_at` from
`clock_timestamp()` and the actor from the authenticated session (A9), calls
`applyChanges`, and commits. **The value change and the obligation to tell
Salesforce are the same commit:** die after it and the row is on disk, die
before and the edit did not happen and the user is told. What creates a queue
row is **condition 8.3, the same one the inbound path uses.**

### 6.2 The worker loop

Appendix C.4 has it. Each tick: hold the leader lease (else idle as a standby,
[ADR 0003](adr/0003-one-sender-with-a-leader-lease.md)); reclaim rows whose
30-second lease expired; probe instead of claiming if the breaker is open; claim
**whole records**, oldest-due first so nothing starves; read current values and
build one call per record; take a governor token; send and settle. `attempts`
rises when a row is **claimed**, not when it fails, so a row that crashes us
mid-send cannot be retried forever.

### 6.3 Coalescing, and reading the value late

All fields owed on one record become **one** call — a four-field form save is
four rows and one PATCH.

> The sender reads each field's **current value at send time**, never a value
> carried on the queue row, which is why part 4 stores none.

A city edit at 09:00 and another at 11:00 during an outage send **the 11:00
value, once.** On a `2xx`, **after** the response and never before, the sender
sets `sf_value` and `sf_observed_at` to what it sent — *our own write is the most
recent thing we know about Salesforce's state* — writes the `echo_fence` rows,
and records `sent_at`. Appendix B traces the divergence that first step prevents.

### 6.4 The cap, slowing down, and the breaker

**70 of the 100 req/s,** both bounds chosen. *Not 100:* the cap counts our
retries and belongs to the client's org, so another integration's burst would
reach us as rejections, while at 70 a 30% burst is absorbed. *Not lower:*
catch-up scales inversely — 10.4 row 1 drains in 6.3 min, row 5 at a governor of
25 takes 16.0. Steady state spends ~7.4 req/s, so we run at **11% utilisation**
and the other 89% drains backlogs.

**On a slow-down signal** (A8), nothing is dropped:

```
rate := max(5, rate / 2)                   -- multiplicative decrease
row.state := 'pending'
row.next_attempt_at := now + (Retry-After, else 2^attempts s with jitter, cap 300 s)
row.attempts := attempts - 1               -- given back: not the row's fault
recover: rate := min(70, rate + 5) per 30 s of clean responses
```

**The breaker splits two failures, and that split is what makes a 6-hour outage
survivable.** An **endpoint failure** (refused, timeout, 5xx) says nothing about
the row: after 5 consecutive ones we stop claiming and probe every 30 s, claimed
rows return to `pending` **with attempts restored**, and on close we resume at
half rate and ramp. A **row failure** — a 400-class rejection naming this
record's data — is the only kind counting attempts toward giving up. Without the
split, 10 attempts at a 5-minute cap is under an hour, so a 6-hour outage would
mark its whole backlog `failed`.

### 6.5 Restart, and settling a group

A restart is a non-event: the new process takes the lease, reclaims rows whose
lease expired, and resumes. A row that reached Salesforce before the crash is
sent again, which is safe because all three calls are idempotent (C.1).

| Outcome | State | Attempts | Then |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `2xx` | `sent` | — | set `sf_value`/`sf_observed_at`; write `echo_fence`; record `sent_at` |
| `429` / limit | `pending` | restored | halve the rate; honour `Retry-After` |
| timeout / refused / `5xx` | `pending` | restored | counts toward the breaker; backoff with jitter |
| `400`-class, data rejected | `failed` | kept | **alert** — a value the portal accepts and Salesforce refuses needs a human |
| `404`, record gone | `failed` | kept | **alert** — deletes are out of scope (A15) |
| `401` / `403` | `pending` | restored | **page, stop the sender** — bad credentials would otherwise burn the queue into `failed` |

A `failed` row is never deleted; it keeps its `last_error`.

---

## 7. The rule when both sides change the same record

### 7.1 Who is doing the merging

**Salesforce has no merge logic**, so our database holds the decision. Hence the
rule that is easy to miss: **a webhook we reject is not a no-op.** It is the
discovery that Salesforce holds a value we rejected, and since nobody else will
fix that, it owes an outbound call (8.3).

### 7.2 The order key — the field that decides which edit is current

| Component | On a webhook | On a portal save |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `occurred_at` | **the payload's `occurredAt`** | **`clock_timestamp()` of the saving transaction** (A9) |
| `origin_rank` | `1` | `0` |
| `origin_event_id` | **the payload's `eventId`** | the portal change id, a ULID per save |

> **Apply the incoming change if and only if its order key is strictly greater
> than the stored one.**

`clock_timestamp()`, not `now()`, which returns the transaction's start. On an
exact tie Salesforce wins, the cheaper direction, since a losing Salesforce value
owes a repair write and a losing portal value owes nothing; a shared millisecond
(A11) then breaks on `origin_event_id`, arbitrarily but **stably**, because
redelivered events must rank the same way twice. Strictness is load-bearing:
`>` and not `>=` makes re-applying an applied change a no-op, so the inbound path
is idempotent independently of the duplicate table.

### 7.3 Canonical form

Canonicalised **before** being compared or stored; the stored form is canonical.

| Field | Canonical form |
| --- | --- |
| all text | Unicode NFC; trim; collapse internal whitespace runs to one space |
| `email` | the above, then lowercased whole |
| `phone` | E.164 by the contact's country; on a parse failure, digits with a leading `+`, and raise the parse-failure counter |
| `status` | mapped through the agreed picklist vocabulary |
| `customer_id` | the `portal_id` UUID, lowercase hex |
| empty | `''` and `NULL` are one thing, stored `NULL` |

Not hygiene — this is what makes part 9 true. **One formatting difference between
the two systems reads as a change, and turns the sync into a generator of its own
traffic** (F.7).

### 7.4 Different fields — the brief's own scenario

No conflict rule needed, which is the argument for ADR 0002. Finance sets `city`;
`phone` is untouched. Sales changes `phone`; the webhook names `phone` only (A3),
so `city` is never looked at. The portal ends with the new phone **and** the
finance city, each with its own actor and time. Appendix A traces it with the
echo in place.

### 7.5 The same field

**Across the two sides:** the order key decides; the winner gets an `applied`
row; **the loser is kept** as `superseded` with its value, actor and time (the
brief is explicit that the fact of an earlier edit stays on record); and **if the
loser was Salesforce's value, a repair write is enqueued** (8.3).

**Two portal users, same field:** the record lock makes the saves serialise
rather than tie, so the second wins on a later `clock_timestamp()` and the
first's value survives in `field_change` under their name. What they *see* is a
product decision (open question 4); my rule is that the portal re-reads after a
save, renders each field as "set by X at T", and shows an inline notice naming
who replaced a value the user submitted — **no blocking and no merge dialog.**

### 7.6 Two clocks: the rule for the skew window

7.2 compares Salesforce's clock against ours, so inside the skew window (A10:
2 s) an edit made second can rank first.

> **The order key stays authoritative inside the window; we do not detect or
> correct an inversion. We bound the skew, and we measure and page on the
> inversions.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Bound** | hosts run NTP; drift above **500 ms** is a host alarm, so at most a quarter of A10's 2 s is ours |
| **Measure** | **cross-side near-tie inversions/hour** — `superseded` rows whose superseding change has the opposite `origin` and `abs(Δ occurred_at) ≤ 2 s`; the precise form of part 11's third number |
| **Warn / page** | 5/hour; **20/hour**, or any rolling 4-hour window where **≥ 80%** of inversions favour one origin |

The bias threshold does the work: genuine races go both ways, so a sustained
one-directional result is the signature of real skew and would sit under any
volume threshold indefinitely. **No deterministic in-window tiebreak** is
offered, because both candidates are worse than the inversion they fix, and
being wrong is bounded (F.7).

## 8. Duplicates and out-of-order changes

### 8.1 A duplicate webhook

**`eventId` is the idempotency key, claimed in the same transaction as the
apply.** No row from the `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` means we have seen it: commit,
answer `200 {"status":"duplicate"}`, change nothing. Salesforce has done nothing
wrong (A7), so this is counted, not alerted.

Two independent layers, **and only the second is the guarantee:**
*suppression*, the table, so a duplicate does no work; and *harmlessness*, the
strict `>` of 7.2, which makes re-applying a change whose order key equals the
stored one do nothing even unsuppressed. Layer 1 falls to a prune, a restore or a
truncate; layer 2 holds regardless — **a design resting on the table alone is one
retention policy away from corrupting data.** Two details: a repeated `eventId`
with a *different* `payload_hash` is a provider bug, so first write wins and this
one **is** alerted; and **a duplicate is not an echo** — a duplicate is one event
twice under one `eventId`, an echo a distinct event describing our own write.

### 8.2 An older webhook after a newer one

> **Compare order keys per field; a change not strictly newer never becomes
> current, and is recorded `superseded`.**

```
evt_A  phone -> ...0001  occurredAt 11:30:04.000    evt_B  phone -> ...0002  11:30:09.000

B first:  11:30:09 > stored           -> APPLIED. current ...0002,
                                         sf_value ...0002, sf_observed_at 11:30:09
A second: (a) 11:30:04 NOT > 11:30:09 -> sf_value LEFT ALONE (a later SF state is known)
          (c) 11:30:04 < 11:30:09     -> SUPERSEDED. history keeps ...0001,
                                         sales.user, 11:30:04; current stays ...0002
          (d) sf_value = current      -> NO repair write
```

Step (a) is what makes this correct rather than merely plausible: a repair rule
comparing the incoming value against ours would fire here and waste a call,
because `evt_A` describes a **past** state of Salesforce. **No reordering
buffer** — A11 gives no sequence numbers, so we cannot detect that anything is
*missing*, and a buffer could only add fixed latency to every event.

### 8.3 The repair write — one condition for every case

> **After every field, regardless of what happened to it: if
> `field_version.sf_value` is distinct from the current value, enqueue a repair
> write.**

"Distinct from" is SQL's `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and the NULL case is load-bearing:
**an `sf_value` we have never learned is distinct from any current value**,
because "we do not know what Salesforce holds" is itself a disagreement we owe a
call about. Without it every portal-created record would be stranded.

| What happened | `sf_value` after | Current | Repair? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Salesforce change applied | the new value | the same | no |
| Salesforce value superseded by a newer portal edit | Salesforce's | ours | **yes** |
| older event after a newer one (8.2) | unchanged | matches it | no |
| echo of our own write | what we sent | the same | no |
| Salesforce restates a value we hold | that value | the same | no |
| full-record restatement during an outage (8.4) | Salesforce's stale value | our unsent edit | **yes** |

It **terminates** — the repair sends our current value, the echo sets `sf_value`
to it, the condition goes false — and it is the **entire logic of outage
recovery** (10.3): feed Salesforce's current values in as observations, and the
fields needing repair are those where the condition is true.

### 8.4 If a webhook carries the full record instead

A3 assumes changed-fields-only. **Full-record mode is the dangerous one,**
because a field's silence and its restatement look identical. *The hazard:*
during an outage finance sets `city` to Noida at 15:00, unsent; at 16:00 a sales
user changes the phone and the full-record payload carries `city: "Gurugram"` —
Salesforce's stale copy — stamped 16:00. Compared as a change, `16:00 > 15:00`,
so we would **overwrite the finance edit with an older value Salesforce was
merely restating.**

> *The rule,* step (b) of the apply: **a field whose canonical value equals the
> `sf_value` we already held is a restatement — not restamped, not compared, not
> touched.**

Traced: `sf_value[city]` is already `Gurugram`, so `city` is skipped and stays
Noida, and 8.3 enqueues the repair we already owed; `phone` differs from its
`sf_value` and applies normally. **Step (b) is unconditional**, whatever the
payload shape, which is why `applyChanges` needs no mode parameter — and the
outage sweep (10.3) requires it regardless. Full-record remains the weaker shape,
which is why A3 is the assumption I would most want confirmed in writing (F.8).

---

## 9. The rule that stops a loop

Ranked second of eight: every other failure damages the records it touches, while
a loop consumes the whole 100 req/s budget and stops sync for every record at
once, within seconds of deployment.

**L1 — the structural rule, and the termination guarantee.**

> **Outbound work is created exactly when `field_version.sf_value` differs from a
> field's current value — condition 8.3, after every field, on both paths, and
> nowhere else.**

```
portal sets city = Noida  -> sf_value "Gurugram" <> "Noida"  -> 1 outbound row
we PATCH Noida, 2xx       -> sf_value := "Noida"                            (6.3)
Salesforce echoes Noida   -> sf_value "Noida" = current       -> 0 rows.  Dead.
```

No fuel after one hop — not because a rule caught it, but because there is
nothing left to disagree about. **Precondition: canonical form (7.3).**

**L2 — the actor rule.**

> A webhook whose `changedBy` is the integration user (A6) is an echo: recorded,
> never compared, never applied.

Load-bearing, not economy: L1 guarantees the loop stops, L2 that it stops on the
**right value**. The echo of our own write carries the time Salesforce stored it,
later than the edit that write overwrote, so compared as a change it would win
and launder our value back over a newer edit from the other side — Appendix B
traces exactly that. It also closes part 5's case (c).

**L3 — the echo fence.**

> After a 2xx the sender records the record, field and hash of the canonical
> value sent, expiring in 15 minutes; an inbound change matching an unexpired
> entry is an echo.

L2's guarantee keyed on the value rather than the actor, so it still holds if A6
is false. Safe because the fence is written after the response, so it cannot
exist for a call that did not land.

**L4 — the repair breaker.**

> Above **5 repairs to one field in an hour**, enqueue nothing more for it, mark
> it contested, and alert.

Bounds the one way L1 fails: a value Salesforce stores in a spelling our
canonical form does not normalise makes every echo read as disagreement, and the
two systems argue at one request per round trip forever. When it trips we keep
serving our value and stop arguing.

| | Guarantees | Absent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **L1** + canonical form | the loop **terminates** | everything; no other layer saves us |
| **L2** | it terminates on the **right value** | our own write launders a stale value over a newer one |
| L3 | L2's guarantee without A6 | nothing, while A6 holds |
| L4 | bounds L1's one failure mode | an unbounded argument over one field |

## 10. The 6-hour outage

### 10.1 What it is

Six hours with the Salesforce API unreachable and webhooks sent during it
possibly never arriving — dark both ways at once (A16).

**The arithmetic uses the business-hours average of 3 edits/s, not A1's 20/s
peak.** Saying so up front because the two differ greatly — about 6 minutes
against about 35 — and the choice is a judgement, not an oversight: a peak is a
15-minute phenomenon, and six consecutive hours of one is not credible. The peak
is carried as row 3 of 10.4, so both numbers are on the page.

**The portal keeps working throughout:** edits apply locally, appear at once, and
queue for Salesforce. The only cost is visibility in Salesforce, and the
30-second target does not apply during catch-up.

### 10.2 What is on disk

| | At the worst moment | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `outbound_change`, `pending` | **19,440 rows, ~4.9 MB** | each committed in the same transaction as the edit that caused it (6.1) |
| rows left `inflight` by a restart | a handful | reclaimed when the 30-second lease expires |
| `sync_watermark` | one row per object type | where the sweep resumes |

Five megabytes is what "pending calls must still be there after our process
restarts" costs. **A restart during the outage is a non-event:** rows are
committed so they survive, leases expire and rows return to `pending`, the
breaker reopens on its probes. Nothing needs a human.

### 10.3 How we drain it — and why the order is not negotiable

> **The inbound sweep must complete before the outbound drain begins.**

The loss it prevents: finance sets a city to Noida at 15:00, queued unsent; at
17:00 a sales user sets it to Delhi in Salesforce and that webhook never arrives;
the link returns at 21:00. *Drain first:* we PATCH Noida, Delhi is overwritten,
and the sweep then reads back our own value — **Delhi is destroyed with no record
it existed.** *Sweep first:* Delhi's `SystemModstamp` of 17:00 beats the portal's
15:00, Noida is kept as `superseded` under the finance user's name, 8.3 finds
nothing owed, and the queued row then sends the **current** value (6.3) — Delhi,
a no-op. Both edits on record, both copies agreeing.

With 14,954 portal-touched and 34,892 Salesforce-touched records out of 5 M
(row 1), the expected overlap is `14,954 × 34,892 / 5,000,000` = **104 records**.
The ordering costs no time and protects exactly those.

**The sweep depends on the restatement rule and could not work without it:** a
`SystemModstamp` is a *record's* modification time, so a record touched at 17:00
hands back every field stamped 17:00, including fields last changed months ago,
which compared as changes would beat any portal edit made during the outage.
Step (b) of 8.4 stops it.

The sequence is Appendix C.5: probe, hold the drain, page through the
changed-since query feeding each record in as a full-record observation, advance
the watermark per page so a crash resumes at a page boundary, then release the
drain at half rate. The drain skips what the sweep resolved by dropping at claim
time any row whose field already has `sf_value` equal to the current value.

### 10.4 The arithmetic — every figure, in one table

**The shared derivation, written once.** Every number in this document comes out
of these lines; the table varies one assumption per row.

```

queued changes   portal edits/s x 21,600
outbound calls   queued changes / 1.3 changes per record      (coalescing, 6.3)
drain capacity   governor - 7.4 req/s reserved for live traffic
                 (7.4 = peak steady state: (6 + 0.7 repairs) x 1.1 retries, 6.4)
drain            resume at half the governor, +5 req/s every 30 s, then full capacity
sweep            Salesforce records / 2,000 per SOQL page     (requests)
                 Salesforce records / 500 per second          (local apply)
total            sweep + drain  -- the sweep blocks the drain (10.3)
```

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **base** | — | 0.90 | 19,440 | 14,954 | 5.1 | 34,892 | 18 | 1.2 | **6.3** |

**On the dashboard but not paging:** the governor's rate and 429 count, the
breaker's state, rows in `failed` and fields marked contested, signature failures

edit the same records in the portal Tequity built on Postgres. Both copies must
agree within 30 seconds while both are up, every field's history must be kept,

## Summary

The unit of sync is a **field**, not a record. Each field carries an **order
key** `(occurred_at, origin_rank, origin_event_id)`; the current value is the
one whose key is greatest.

**Salesforce has no merge logic** — it overwrites with whatever lands last. We
are the only party that compares anything, so our database holds the decision
and Salesforce's copy is a projection of it. Hence the one rule everything
follows from:

> **Outbound work is created exactly when `sf_value` — what we believe
> Salesforce holds for a field — differs from that field's current value.**
> Checked after every field, on both paths, nowhere else.
> *We call Salesforce when, and only when, we believe Salesforce disagrees with us.*

| Rule | | § |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Duplicate** | `eventId` claimed in the apply's own transaction; and the compare is strictly `>`, so a duplicate escaping the table is a no-op anyway | 8.1 |
| **Out of order** | order keys compared per field; a change not strictly newer never becomes current, and is kept as `superseded` with its actor and time | 8.2 |
| **Loop** | an echo makes `sf_value` equal the current value, so the condition goes false — no fuel after one hop | 9 |
| **6-h outage** | queue rows commit with the edit, so they survive a restart; on recovery the inbound sweep runs **before** the outbound drain | 10.3 |

**Numbers.** Peak 20 edits/s assumed, business-hours average 3, quiet hour 0.5.
We run at **70 of the 100 req/s** allowed, 11% used in steady state. A 6-hour
outage queues **19,440 changes → 14,954 calls**, draining in 5.1 min; with the
1.2-min sweep first, **6.3 min** (row 1, 10.4). The 30-second target closes at
~6 s both ways, 7 of the 9.8 worst-case seconds being Salesforce's.

| **S4** | make inbound delivery safe to repeat and to reorder | cannot be earlier ("older" needs S1's key); severe but detectable and replayable | **yes** |
| **S5** | know which record is which across the systems | a lost create response can duplicate a record: bad, but bounded and visible at once | no |
| **S6** | recover what was missed while a side was dark | **first to ask about**, sixth to build: fixed by re-running, but rests on A4 | no |
| **S7** | prove the webhook came from Salesforce | a gate, not a risk; stubbed day one, filled before production | no |
| **S8** | load the 5 million existing records | one-off, offline, no latency target, re-runnable | no |

**The demo exercises S1–S4 and nothing below** — exactly the four whose failures
are unrecoverable or silent: phone-and-city with full history (S1), our own
update returning and not being sent back (S2), a pending call surviving a restart
with Salesforce down and then draining under an enforced cap (S3), a duplicate
and an older event after a newer one (S4). S2, S6, S7 and S8 add **no process**.

## 4. The data we store

Eight tables; Appendix C.2 has the DDL.
[ADR 0002](adr/0002-merge-per-field-not-per-record.md): **the unit of sync is a
field** — forced, since the brief's scenario has a portal city edit and a
Salesforce phone edit concurrent with each other, and a record-level comparison
must discard one, unable to see they touched different fields.

| Table | Holds | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `customer`, `contact` | **the current values**, typed | they live **here and nowhere else** |
| `field_version` | the **order key** per `(record, field)`, plus `sf_value` / `sf_observed_at` — what we believe Salesforce holds. Moved by a Salesforce observation **and by our own successful send** | a **cache, not a second truth**; also the row MERGE locks |
| `field_change` | **the history**: append-only, `applied` and `superseded`, both **permanent** | what the client is buying; `superseded` stays because the brief says an earlier edit stays on record |
| `sync_observation` | `echo`, `confirmed`, `restatement`; 90-day partitions | not edits by people, so not history |
| `inbound_event` | the duplicate key, 30-day retention (104 MB) | 8.1 |
| `outbound_change` | the **durable queue** — which field is owed, **never the value** | 6.3 |
| `record_link` | Salesforce id ↔ portal id, and the per-record lock | a portal-created record has a `portal_id` first |
| `echo_fence`, `sync_watermark` | "we just wrote this" (15-min TTL); how far through Salesforce's history we are sure | 9, 10.3 |

**Does the storage close?** 5 M typed rows at 1.2 GB; **27 M** `field_version`
rows (1 M × 3 fields + 4 M × 6) at 5.5 GB with its index; `field_change` at
**26 M rows/year** (20 M edits × 1.3 fields) and **5.2 GB/yr, kept forever
because it is the product**. **~13 GB in year one, growing 5 GB/yr.**

## 5. The inbound path

**One HTTP request becomes one Postgres transaction**, with no network call
inside it and no background step. The sequence is Appendix C.3: validate, claim
the `eventId`, lock the record, then per field **(a) learn → (b) restatement →
(c) decide → (d) repair**, then commit and answer 200.

- **(a) learn** records what Salesforce holds regardless of what (c) decides,
  which is what collapses repair into the single condition 8.3.
- **(b) restatement** skips a field restating the `sf_value` we already held
  (8.4).
- **(c) decide** takes the first case that applies — echo, then
  value-already-equal (`confirmed`), then the order-key comparison, then
  `superseded` — and only here can a current value change.
- **(d) repair** is condition 8.3, after every field whatever happened to it.

Three properties are deliberate. **The duplicate claim and the apply share one
transaction** — split them and a crash between marks an event processed that was
never applied, which Salesforce will never resend (A7 promises redelivery only
until we answer 200). **No network call is inside it**, keeping the endpoint's
p99 at 200 ms. **Fields are independent** — one event may apply `phone` and
supersede `city`, and the event's own outcome is then `partial`.

> A change whose canonical value already equals the current value changes
> **nothing** — not the value, not the order key, and not history.

| Resolving the record | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** known `sf_id` | one indexed lookup, lock, proceed |
| **(b)** unknown `sf_id`, `changedBy` a human | a Salesforce-created record we have not seen: mint a `portal_id`, insert the link and an empty row, apply every field as a first write. **Recovery (10.3) reuses this path** |
| **(c)** unknown `sf_id`, `changedBy` the integration user | the echo of a create *we* made, arriving before we recorded the id it returned. **Answer 503 + `Retry-After: 5`, apply nothing** — by the redelivery it is case (a). Bounded: after 60 s log loudly and treat as (b) |

**400 versus 500**, since a 400 discards the event forever: an unknown *field
name* earns one; a *value* we failed to canonicalise is our bug and earns a 500.

## 6. The outbound path

### 6.1 The portal save

The handler takes the same record lock as part 5, stamps `occurred_at` from
`clock_timestamp()` and the actor from the authenticated session (A9), calls
`applyChanges`, and commits. **The value change and the obligation to tell
Salesforce are the same commit:** die after it and the row is on disk, die
before and the edit did not happen and the user is told. What creates a queue
row is **condition 8.3, the same one the inbound path uses.**

### 6.2 The worker loop

Appendix C.4 has it. Each tick: hold the leader lease (else idle as a standby,
[ADR 0003](adr/0003-one-sender-with-a-leader-lease.md)); reclaim rows whose
30-second lease expired; probe instead of claiming if the breaker is open; claim
**whole records**, oldest-due first so nothing starves; read current values and
build one call per record; take a governor token; send and settle. `attempts`
rises when a row is **claimed**, not when it fails, so a row that crashes us
mid-send cannot be retried forever.

### 6.3 Coalescing, and reading the value late

All fields owed on one record become **one** call — a four-field form save is
four rows and one PATCH.

> The sender reads each field's **current value at send time**, never a value
> carried on the queue row, which is why part 4 stores none.

A city edit at 09:00 and another at 11:00 during an outage send **the 11:00
value, once.** On a `2xx`, **after** the response and never before, the sender
sets `sf_value` and `sf_observed_at` to what it sent — *our own write is the most
recent thing we know about Salesforce's state* — writes the `echo_fence` rows,
and records `sent_at`. Appendix B traces the divergence that first step prevents.

### 6.4 The cap, slowing down, and the breaker

**70 of the 100 req/s,** both bounds chosen. *Not 100:* the cap counts our
retries and belongs to the client's org, so another integration's burst would
reach us as rejections, while at 70 a 30% burst is absorbed. *Not lower:*
catch-up scales inversely — 10.4 row 1 drains in 6.3 min, row 5 at a governor of
25 takes 16.0. Steady state spends ~7.4 req/s, so we run at **11% utilisation**
and the other 89% drains backlogs.

**On a slow-down signal** (A8), nothing is dropped:

```
rate := max(5, rate / 2)                   -- multiplicative decrease
row.state := 'pending'
row.next_attempt_at := now + (Retry-After, else 2^attempts s with jitter, cap 300 s)
row.attempts := attempts - 1               -- given back: not the row's fault
recover: rate := min(70, rate + 5) per 30 s of clean responses
```

**The breaker splits two failures, and that split is what makes a 6-hour outage
survivable.** An **endpoint failure** (refused, timeout, 5xx) says nothing about
the row: after 5 consecutive ones we stop claiming and probe every 30 s, claimed
rows return to `pending` **with attempts restored**, and on close we resume at
half rate and ramp. A **row failure** — a 400-class rejection naming this
record's data — is the only kind counting attempts toward giving up. Without the
split, 10 attempts at a 5-minute cap is under an hour, so a 6-hour outage would
mark its whole backlog `failed`.

### 6.5 Restart, and settling a group

A restart is a non-event: the new process takes the lease, reclaims rows whose
lease expired, and resumes. A row that reached Salesforce before the crash is
sent again, which is safe because all three calls are idempotent (C.1).

| Outcome | State | Attempts | Then |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `2xx` | `sent` | — | set `sf_value`/`sf_observed_at`; write `echo_fence`; record `sent_at` |
| `429` / limit | `pending` | restored | halve the rate; honour `Retry-After` |
| timeout / refused / `5xx` | `pending` | restored | counts toward the breaker; backoff with jitter |
| `400`-class, data rejected | `failed` | kept | **alert** — a value the portal accepts and Salesforce refuses needs a human |
| `404`, record gone | `failed` | kept | **alert** — deletes are out of scope (A15) |
| `401` / `403` | `pending` | restored | **page, stop the sender** — bad credentials would otherwise burn the queue into `failed` |

A `failed` row is never deleted; it keeps its `last_error`.

## 7. The rule when both sides change the same record

### 7.1 Who is doing the merging

**Salesforce has no merge logic**, so our database holds the decision. Hence the
rule that is easy to miss: **a webhook we reject is not a no-op.** It is the
discovery that Salesforce holds a value we rejected, and since nobody else will
fix that, it owes an outbound call (8.3).

### 7.2 The order key — the field that decides which edit is current

| Component | On a webhook | On a portal save |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `occurred_at` | **the payload's `occurredAt`** | **`clock_timestamp()` of the saving transaction** (A9) |
| `origin_rank` | `1` | `0` |
| `origin_event_id` | **the payload's `eventId`** | the portal change id, a ULID per save |

> **Apply the incoming change if and only if its order key is strictly greater
> than the stored one.**

`clock_timestamp()`, not `now()`, which returns the transaction's start. On an
exact tie Salesforce wins, the cheaper direction, since a losing Salesforce value
owes a repair write and a losing portal value owes nothing; a shared millisecond
(A11) then breaks on `origin_event_id`, arbitrarily but **stably**, because
redelivered events must rank the same way twice. Strictness is load-bearing:
`>` and not `>=` makes re-applying an applied change a no-op, so the inbound path
is idempotent independently of the duplicate table.

### 7.3 Canonical form

Canonicalised **before** being compared or stored; the stored form is canonical.

| Field | Canonical form |
| --- | --- |
| all text | Unicode NFC; trim; collapse internal whitespace runs to one space |
| `email` | the above, then lowercased whole |
| `phone` | E.164 by the contact's country; on a parse failure, digits with a leading `+`, and raise the parse-failure counter |
| `status` | mapped through the agreed picklist vocabulary |
| `customer_id` | the `portal_id` UUID, lowercase hex |
| empty | `''` and `NULL` are one thing, stored `NULL` |

Not hygiene — this is what makes part 9 true. **One formatting difference between
the two systems reads as a change, and turns the sync into a generator of its own
traffic** (F.7).

### 7.4 Different fields — the brief's own scenario

No conflict rule needed, which is the argument for ADR 0002. Finance sets `city`;
`phone` is untouched. Sales changes `phone`; the webhook names `phone` only (A3),
so `city` is never looked at. The portal ends with the new phone **and** the
finance city, each with its own actor and time. Appendix A traces it with the
echo in place.

### 7.5 The same field

**Across the two sides:** the order key decides; the winner gets an `applied`
row; **the loser is kept** as `superseded` with its value, actor and time (the
brief is explicit that the fact of an earlier edit stays on record); and **if the
loser was Salesforce's value, a repair write is enqueued** (8.3).

**Two portal users, same field:** the record lock makes the saves serialise
rather than tie, so the second wins on a later `clock_timestamp()` and the
first's value survives in `field_change` under their name. What they *see* is a
product decision (open question 4); my rule is that the portal re-reads after a
save, renders each field as "set by X at T", and shows an inline notice naming
who replaced a value the user submitted — **no blocking and no merge dialog.**

### 7.6 Two clocks: the rule for the skew window

7.2 compares Salesforce's clock against ours, so inside the skew window (A10:
2 s) an edit made second can rank first.

> **The order key stays authoritative inside the window; we do not detect or
> correct an inversion. We bound the skew, and we measure and page on the
> inversions.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Bound** | hosts run NTP; drift above **500 ms** is a host alarm, so at most a quarter of A10's 2 s is ours |
| **Measure** | **cross-side near-tie inversions/hour** — `superseded` rows whose superseding change has the opposite `origin` and `abs(Δ occurred_at) ≤ 2 s`; the precise form of part 11's third number |
| **Warn / page** | 5/hour; **20/hour**, or any rolling 4-hour window where **≥ 80%** of inversions favour one origin |

The bias threshold does the work: genuine races go both ways, so a sustained
one-directional result is the signature of real skew and would sit under any
volume threshold indefinitely. **No deterministic in-window tiebreak** is
offered, because both candidates are worse than the inversion they fix, and
being wrong is bounded (F.7).

## 8. Duplicates and out-of-order changes

### 8.1 A duplicate webhook

**`eventId` is the idempotency key, claimed in the same transaction as the
apply.** No row from the `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` means we have seen it: commit,
answer `200 {"status":"duplicate"}`, change nothing. Salesforce has done nothing
wrong (A7), so this is counted, not alerted.

Two independent layers, **and only the second is the guarantee:**
*suppression*, the table, so a duplicate does no work; and *harmlessness*, the
strict `>` of 7.2, which makes re-applying a change whose order key equals the
stored one do nothing even unsuppressed. Layer 1 falls to a prune, a restore or a
truncate; layer 2 holds regardless — **a design resting on the table alone is one
retention policy away from corrupting data.** Two details: a repeated `eventId`
with a *different* `payload_hash` is a provider bug, so first write wins and this
one **is** alerted; and **a duplicate is not an echo** — a duplicate is one event
twice under one `eventId`, an echo a distinct event describing our own write.

### 8.2 An older webhook after a newer one

> **Compare order keys per field; a change not strictly newer never becomes
> current, and is recorded `superseded`.**

```
evt_A  phone -> ...0001  occurredAt 11:30:04.000    evt_B  phone -> ...0002  11:30:09.000

B first:  11:30:09 > stored           -> APPLIED. current ...0002,
                                         sf_value ...0002, sf_observed_at 11:30:09
A second: (a) 11:30:04 NOT > 11:30:09 -> sf_value LEFT ALONE (a later SF state is known)
          (c) 11:30:04 < 11:30:09     -> SUPERSEDED. history keeps ...0001,
                                         sales.user, 11:30:04; current stays ...0002
          (d) sf_value = current      -> NO repair write
```

Step (a) is what makes this correct rather than merely plausible: a repair rule
comparing the incoming value against ours would fire here and waste a call,
because `evt_A` describes a **past** state of Salesforce. **No reordering
buffer** — A11 gives no sequence numbers, so we cannot detect that anything is
*missing*, and a buffer could only add fixed latency to every event.

### 8.3 The repair write — one condition for every case

> **After every field, regardless of what happened to it: if
> `field_version.sf_value` is distinct from the current value, enqueue a repair
> write.**

"Distinct from" is SQL's `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and the NULL case is load-bearing:
**an `sf_value` we have never learned is distinct from any current value**,
because "we do not know what Salesforce holds" is itself a disagreement we owe a
call about. Without it every portal-created record would be stranded.

| What happened | `sf_value` after | Current | Repair? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Salesforce change applied | the new value | the same | no |
| Salesforce value superseded by a newer portal edit | Salesforce's | ours | **yes** |
| older event after a newer one (8.2) | unchanged | matches it | no |
| echo of our own write | what we sent | the same | no |
| Salesforce restates a value we hold | that value | the same | no |
| full-record restatement during an outage (8.4) | Salesforce's stale value | our unsent edit | **yes** |

It **terminates** — the repair sends our current value, the echo sets `sf_value`
to it, the condition goes false — and it is the **entire logic of outage
recovery** (10.3): feed Salesforce's current values in as observations, and the
fields needing repair are those where the condition is true.

### 8.4 If a webhook carries the full record instead

A3 assumes changed-fields-only. **Full-record mode is the dangerous one,**
because a field's silence and its restatement look identical. *The hazard:*
during an outage finance sets `city` to Noida at 15:00, unsent; at 16:00 a sales
user changes the phone and the full-record payload carries `city: "Gurugram"` —
Salesforce's stale copy — stamped 16:00. Compared as a change, `16:00 > 15:00`,
so we would **overwrite the finance edit with an older value Salesforce was
merely restating.**

> *The rule,* step (b) of the apply: **a field whose canonical value equals the
> `sf_value` we already held is a restatement — not restamped, not compared, not
> touched.**

Traced: `sf_value[city]` is already `Gurugram`, so `city` is skipped and stays
Noida, and 8.3 enqueues the repair we already owed; `phone` differs from its
`sf_value` and applies normally. **Step (b) is unconditional**, whatever the
payload shape, which is why `applyChanges` needs no mode parameter — and the
outage sweep (10.3) requires it regardless. Full-record remains the weaker shape,
which is why A3 is the assumption I would most want confirmed in writing (F.8).

## 9. The rule that stops a loop

Ranked second of eight: every other failure damages the records it touches, while
a loop consumes the whole 100 req/s budget and stops sync for every record at
once, within seconds of deployment.

**L1 — the structural rule, and the termination guarantee.**

> **Outbound work is created exactly when `field_version.sf_value` differs from a
> field's current value — condition 8.3, after every field, on both paths, and
> nowhere else.**

```
portal sets city = Noida  -> sf_value "Gurugram" <> "Noida"  -> 1 outbound row
we PATCH Noida, 2xx       -> sf_value := "Noida"                            (6.3)
Salesforce echoes Noida   -> sf_value "Noida" = current       -> 0 rows.  Dead.
```

No fuel after one hop — not because a rule caught it, but because there is
nothing left to disagree about. **Precondition: canonical form (7.3).**

**L2 — the actor rule.**

> A webhook whose `changedBy` is the integration user (A6) is an echo: recorded,
> never compared, never applied.

Load-bearing, not economy: L1 guarantees the loop stops, L2 that it stops on the
**right value**. The echo of our own write carries the time Salesforce stored it,
later than the edit that write overwrote, so compared as a change it would win
and launder our value back over a newer edit from the other side — Appendix B
traces exactly that. It also closes part 5's case (c).

**L3 — the echo fence.**

> After a 2xx the sender records the record, field and hash of the canonical
> value sent, expiring in 15 minutes; an inbound change matching an unexpired
> entry is an echo.

L2's guarantee keyed on the value rather than the actor, so it still holds if A6
is false. Safe because the fence is written after the response, so it cannot
exist for a call that did not land.

**L4 — the repair breaker.**

> Above **5 repairs to one field in an hour**, enqueue nothing more for it, mark
> it contested, and alert.

Bounds the one way L1 fails: a value Salesforce stores in a spelling our
canonical form does not normalise makes every echo read as disagreement, and the
two systems argue at one request per round trip forever. When it trips we keep
serving our value and stop arguing.

| | Guarantees | Absent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **L1** + canonical form | the loop **terminates** | everything; no other layer saves us |
| **L2** | it terminates on the **right value** | our own write launders a stale value over a newer one |
| L3 | L2's guarantee without A6 | nothing, while A6 holds |
| L4 | bounds L1's one failure mode | an unbounded argument over one field |

## 10. The 6-hour outage

### 10.1 What it is

Six hours with the Salesforce API unreachable and webhooks sent during it
possibly never arriving — dark both ways at once (A16).

**The arithmetic uses the business-hours average of 3 edits/s, not A1's 20/s
peak.** Saying so up front because the two differ greatly — about 6 minutes
against about 35 — and the choice is a judgement, not an oversight: a peak is a
15-minute phenomenon, and six consecutive hours of one is not credible. The peak
is carried as row 3 of 10.4, so both numbers are on the page.

**The portal keeps working throughout:** edits apply locally, appear at once, and
queue for Salesforce. The only cost is visibility in Salesforce, and the
30-second target does not apply during catch-up.

### 10.2 What is on disk

| | At the worst moment | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `outbound_change`, `pending` | **19,440 rows, ~4.9 MB** | each committed in the same transaction as the edit that caused it (6.1) |
| rows left `inflight` by a restart | a handful | reclaimed when the 30-second lease expires |
| `sync_watermark` | one row per object type | where the sweep resumes |

Five megabytes is what "pending calls must still be there after our process
restarts" costs. **A restart during the outage is a non-event:** rows are
committed so they survive, leases expire and rows return to `pending`, the
breaker reopens on its probes. Nothing needs a human.

### 10.3 How we drain it — and why the order is not negotiable

> **The inbound sweep must complete before the outbound drain begins.**

The loss it prevents: finance sets a city to Noida at 15:00, queued unsent; at
17:00 a sales user sets it to Delhi in Salesforce and that webhook never arrives;
the link returns at 21:00. *Drain first:* we PATCH Noida, Delhi is overwritten,
and the sweep then reads back our own value — **Delhi is destroyed with no record
it existed.** *Sweep first:* Delhi's `SystemModstamp` of 17:00 beats the portal's
15:00, Noida is kept as `superseded` under the finance user's name, 8.3 finds
nothing owed, and the queued row then sends the **current** value (6.3) — Delhi,
a no-op. Both edits on record, both copies agreeing.

With 14,954 portal-touched and 34,892 Salesforce-touched records out of 5 M
(row 1), the expected overlap is `14,954 × 34,892 / 5,000,000` = **104 records**.
The ordering costs no time and protects exactly those.

**The sweep depends on the restatement rule and could not work without it:** a
`SystemModstamp` is a *record's* modification time, so a record touched at 17:00
hands back every field stamped 17:00, including fields last changed months ago,
which compared as changes would beat any portal edit made during the outage.
Step (b) of 8.4 stops it.

The sequence is Appendix C.5: probe, hold the drain, page through the
changed-since query feeding each record in as a full-record observation, advance
the watermark per page so a crash resumes at a page boundary, then release the
drain at half rate. The drain skips what the sweep resolved by dropping at claim
time any row whose field already has `sf_value` equal to the current value.

### 10.4 The arithmetic — every figure, in one table

**The shared derivation, written once.** Every number in this document comes out
of these lines; the table varies one assumption per row.

```
window           6 h x 3600                                 = 21,600 s
queued changes   portal edits/s x 21,600
outbound calls   queued changes / 1.3 changes per record      (coalescing, 6.3)
drain capacity   governor - 7.4 req/s reserved for live traffic
                 (7.4 = peak steady state: (6 + 0.7 repairs) x 1.1 retries, 6.4)
drain            resume at half the governor, +5 req/s every 30 s, then full capacity
sweep            Salesforce records / 2,000 per SOQL page     (requests)
                 Salesforce records / 500 per second          (local apply)
total            sweep + drain  -- the sweep blocks the drain (10.3)
```

| # | Scenario | What varies | portal /s | queued | calls | drain | SF records | reqs | sweep | **total** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **base** | — | 0.90 | 19,440 | 14,954 | 5.1 | 34,892 | 18 | 1.2 | **6.3** |
| 2 | no coalescing | 1.0 chg/record | 0.90 | 19,440 | 19,440 | 6.3 | 34,892 | 18 | 1.2 | **7.5** |
| 3 | sustained peak | A1 → 20/s | 6.00 | 129,600 | 99,692 | 27.7 | 232,615 | 117 | 7.8 | **35.4** |
| 4 | portal-heavy | A2 → 70% portal | 2.10 | 45,360 | 34,892 | 12.0 | 14,954 | 8 | 0.5 | **12.5** |
| 5 | contended cap | A12 → governor 25 | 0.90 | 19,440 | 14,954 | 14.8 | 34,892 | 18 | 1.2 | **16.0** |
| 6 | no changed-since | A4 false → all 5 M | 0.90 | 19,440 | 14,954 | 5.1 | 5,000,000 | 2,500 | 16.7 | **21.8** |

Drain, sweep and total are minutes. **Row 1 is the answer: about 6 minutes.**

```
Row 1, with the division shown
queued     0.9 x 21,600                             = 19,440 changes
calls      19,440 / 1.3                             = 14,954
capacity   70 - 7.4                                 = 62.6 req/s at full rate
ramp       35,40,45,50,55,60,65 req/s, 30 s each, each minus 7.4:
           (27.6+32.6+37.6+42.6+47.6+52.6+57.6) x 30 = 8,946 calls in 210 s
rest       (14,954 - 8,946) / 62.6                  = 96.0 s
drain      210 + 96.0 = 306.0 s                     = 5.1 minutes
sweep      2.1 x 21,600 / 1.3                       = 34,892 records
           34,892 / 2,000 = 18 requests (0.3 s of budget)
           34,892 / 500   = 69.8 s                  = 1.2 minutes
TOTAL      1.2 + 5.1                                = 6.3 minutes
```

Allow **under 10 minutes** operationally, covering page-fetch latency, retries,
and the breaker needing a few probes to close.

**Beyond row 1.** The **cap is the floor, not our design**: row 3's 99,692 calls
at the full 100 req/s with no reserve is still `997 s = 16.6 min`, so our 30%
reserve costs about 11 minutes in the worst credible case and nothing on our side
beats 16.6 — the trade to put in front of the client (A12). **Row 5 matters
most**, being the only row driven by a number we choose rather than observe.
**Row 6 demotes A4** from load-bearing to preferable, and I would want that sweep
**running nightly regardless of A4**, as the standing net under lost webhooks,
canonicalisation gaps, fields L4 gave up on, and 7.6's inversions.

## 11. Three numbers I would watch

One per failure mode: outbound stuck, inbound slow, and getting it wrong. The
third is the only one that detects incorrectness rather than slowness.

| | Number | Normal | Warn | **Call someone** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **age of the oldest unsent change** — `min(created_at)` over `pending` rows | < 5 s | 60 s | **300 s (5 min)** |
| **2** | **inbound lag** — p99 of `applied_at − occurred_at` over Salesforce-origin rows, last 5 min | < 6 s | 20 s | **> 30 s sustained 5 min** |
| **3** | **divergence** — repairs enqueued + Salesforce-origin `superseded` rows, per minute; **and** 7.6's near-tie inversions per hour | ~0; < 1/h | 10/min; 5/h | **100/min; or 20/h, or ≥ 80% one-directional over 4 h** |

**Age, not depth,** for number 1: 19,000 rows draining fast is healthy and 3 rows
stuck is not. Number 2 deliberately **includes Salesforce's own emission delay**,
because the 30 seconds we promised is end to end. Number 3 is the one I would
least give up: nothing else reports a skew past A10, a canonicalisation gap
turning echoes into changes, a loop rule that stopped working, or a Salesforce
process overwriting portal edits in bulk.

**On the dashboard but not paging:** the governor's rate and 429 count, the
breaker's state, rows in `failed` and fields marked contested, signature failures
and 400s, and `sync_watermark` lag.

---

## 12. What I am leaving out

**Because the exercise says so:** deletes (A15), Salesforce login screens, any
visual UI, a second region, and load testing real Salesforce. Where code exists
it runs against a fake Salesforce I wrote.

**Because I chose to,** each with its cost named: the **initial 5 M backfill**
(S8, costed as row 6 of 10.4 — one-off, offline, and it needs the merge rule
first); **Salesforce auth lifecycle** (mechanical; no design decision rests on
it); **schema-change handling** (L4 degrades an unknown picklist value into a
contested field and an alert rather than a loop); **merging already-duplicated
records** (a pre-existing data-quality problem, not one this sync creates);
**field-level permissions** (open question 6); **objects and fields beyond the
nine** (A14 — a tenth field is configuration); **the portal's overwrite notice**
(7.5's rule and data are designed; the UI is out of scope);
**right-to-erasure against permanent history** (open question 5 — a legal
question first); and **the monitoring plumbing** (part 11 has the queries).

**What I would build first:** S1 and S2 alone for a week — the merge rule, the
history, canonical form, and the one condition — against a fake Salesforce with
no real integration connected. Everything after is plumbing around a decision
that has to be right first. And before writing any of it I would get open
question 1 answered: if the webhook is Change Data Capture, replay ids retire
A11, strengthen 8.2 from ordering-what-arrived to detecting-what-is-missing, and
turn the recovery sweep into a replay. That one answer changes more of this
document than any other.
ENDOFPART

# Two-way sync of customer and contact records

**Design document — Tequity Round 1**

Sales edits customers and contacts in Salesforce; finance and customer-success
edit the same records in the portal Tequity built on Postgres. Both copies must
agree within 30 seconds while both are up, every field's history must be kept,
and we control only our side.

This document is the decisions and the numbers. Parts 7–10 are the four rules
and all arithmetic is one table in 10.4; the argument behind each rule is in
[`design-appendix.md`](design-appendix.md), section by section, together with
the brief's scenario traced (**A**), the hardest race traced (**B**),
interfaces, schema DDL and sequences (**C**), each assumption derived with what
changes if it is wrong (**D**), and what the demo substitutes for (**E**).
`docs/adr/` has the three decisions expensive to reverse.

---

## Summary

The unit of sync is a **field**, not a record. Each field carries an **order
key** `(occurred_at, origin_rank, origin_event_id)`; the current value is the
one whose key is greatest.

**Salesforce has no merge logic** — it overwrites with whatever lands last. We
are the only party that compares anything, so our database holds the decision
and Salesforce's copy is a projection of it. Hence the one rule everything
follows from:

> **Outbound work is created exactly when `sf_value` — what we believe
> Salesforce holds for a field — differs from that field's current value.**
> Checked after every field, on both paths, nowhere else.
> *We call Salesforce when, and only when, we believe Salesforce disagrees with us.*

| Rule | | § |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Duplicate** | `eventId` claimed in the apply's own transaction; and the compare is strictly `>`, so a duplicate escaping the table is a no-op anyway | 8.1 |
| **Out of order** | order keys compared per field; a change not strictly newer never becomes current, and is kept as `superseded` with its actor and time | 8.2 |
| **Loop** | an echo makes `sf_value` equal the current value, so the condition goes false — no fuel after one hop | 9 |
| **6-h outage** | queue rows commit with the edit, so they survive a restart; on recovery the inbound sweep runs **before** the outbound drain | 10.3 |

**Numbers.** Peak 20 edits/s assumed, business-hours average 3, quiet hour 0.5.
We run at **70 of the 100 req/s** allowed, 11% used in steady state. A 6-hour
outage queues **19,440 changes → 14,954 calls**, draining in 5.1 min; with the
1.2-min sweep first, **6.3 min** (row 1, 10.4). The 30-second target closes at
~6 s both ways, 7 of the 9.8 worst-case seconds being Salesforce's.

---

## 1. Assumptions, and the questions I would ask

Nothing below was given. **Appendix D derives each one and says what changes if
it goes the other way.** The five the exercise names are A1, A3, A4, A7, A9;
**A4 and A5 assume Salesforce APIs the brief does not mention.**

| | Assumption |
| --- | --- |
| **A1** | **Peak 20 edits/s, business-hours average 3/s, quiet hour 0.5/s** (5 M records × ~4 touches/yr, 250-day 8-hour year, × 7 for peak). **10.4 uses the average; 10.1 says why** |
| **A2** | 70% of edits originate in Salesforce, 30% in the portal |
| **A3** | **A webhook carries only the changed fields**, per the sample |
| **A4** | **Salesforce can be queried for records changed in a window** — SOQL on `SystemModstamp`, 2,000 records/request. **Assumed, not given** |
| **A5** | **Creates can be made idempotent** by external-id upsert on our `portalId`. **Assumed, not given** |
| **A6** | `changedBy` names the API caller, so our integration user is recognisable in it |
| **A7** | **Delivery is at-least-once**; HTTPS, HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, retried on 5xx or timeout |
| **A8** | Throttling arrives as 429 or `REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, with `Retry-After` when available |
| **A9** | **On a portal save the time is our `clock_timestamp()` and the actor is the authenticated session** — never the body's `editedBy`, which a caller could forge |
| **A10** | Clock skew between the two clocks is at most 2 s |
| **A11** | `occurredAt` is UTC, millisecond resolution; two edits can share a millisecond |
| **A12** | The 100 req/s cap is ours alone to spend, and **we run at 70** |
| **A13** | Salesforce emits a webhook within 5 s p99; a record write returns within 2 s p99 |
| **A14** | The nine named fields are the whole schema |
| **A15** | No record is ever deleted (the exercise's scope) |
| **A16** | **The outage is dark both ways at once** — the brief's two sentences jointly imply it, and it is the harder reading |

**Questions I could not close with an assumption.**

1. **How is the webhook produced** — Apex callout, Platform Event, Change Data
   Capture, middleware? Decides A4, A6 and A11 together. Highest-value question.
2. **Is there an external-id field on Account and Contact we may write?** (A5.)
3. **What else in the client's org spends the API limit?** (A12; row 5, 10.4.)
4. **When two portal users edit one field, what should the second see?** 7.5 is
   my rule, but the choice is a product decision.
5. **Must history be retained legally, and does that conflict with
   right-to-erasure?** Part 4 never deletes a change.
6. **Is any field single-owner?** I assume not; if some are, part 7 simplifies
   for them and we need a per-field ownership table.

---

## 2. The systems, who calls whom, the network seam, the interfaces

```
 sales user                  finance / customer-success user
     | edits in                          | edits in
     v                                   v
+--------------+             +--------------------+
|  SALESFORCE  |             |  TEQUITY PORTAL    |
| their CRM+DB |             |  our app           |
+--------------+             +--------------------+
   |      ^                         | in-process
   |      |                         v
   |      |     +-------------------------------------+
   |      |     | MERGE  order keys, history, echo    |
   |      |     |        and repair decisions         |
   |      |     +-------------------------------------+
   |      |            |                     ^
   |      |            v                     |
   |      |     +-------------------------------------+
   |      |     | POSTGRES  records, field history,   |
   |      |     |           outbound queue            |
   |      |     +-------------------------------------+
   |      |           ^                       |
   | == PUBLIC INTERNET == the only path      v
   |      | (A) SF->us                 +-----------------+
   |      |      HTTPS webhook         | SYNC WORKER     |
   +------|------------> [EP] ---------| governor,       |
          | (B) us->SF                 | retries, sweep  |
          +----------------------------+-----------------+
            HTTPS record API: create / update / changed-since

 [EP] WEBHOOK ENDPOINT (ours): validate, dedupe, MERGE, commit, 200.
```

| Path | Caller | Callee | Trigger | Cap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | Salesforce | our webhook endpoint | a record changed in Salesforce | none — inbound is outside the cap |
| **B** | our sync worker | Salesforce record API | we believe Salesforce disagrees with us | 100 req/s hard; we run at 70 |
| — | the portal's save handler | MERGE, in-process | a portal user saved | not a network call |

No human crosses the internet seam; only paths A and B do.

**Two processes, one repository, and the seam between them is Postgres** — not
HTTP, not a broker ([ADR 0001](adr/0001-two-processes-with-postgres-as-the-seam.md)).
The endpoint must never block on Salesforce, and the worker is the single
governor of a shared cap. In one database the inbound apply and the outbound
enqueue are **one commit**, so "we changed a value" and "we owe Salesforce a
call" cannot disagree after a crash.

| Crosses the boundary | Written by | Read by | Means |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `outbound_change` | endpoint and portal, in the merge transaction | sync worker | "we believe Salesforce disagrees about this field" |
| `echo_fence` | sync worker, after a successful send | endpoint | "we just wrote this value; expect it back" |

**The interface on each side is Appendix C.1**: our endpoint's contract and
status codes, the three Salesforce operations we depend on — each idempotent **by
design**, which is what makes at-least-once sending safe — and `applyChanges`,
the one interface every edit path goes through. **A 200 is returned only after
our transaction commits.**

**Does 30 seconds close?** Yes, at ~6 s both ways:

| Portal → Salesforce | p99 | Salesforce → portal | p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| commit (queue row is in it) | — | Salesforce emits (A13, **not ours**) | 5.0 s |
| worker notices (`NOTIFY`, 1 s poll fallback) | 1.0 s | network | 0.5 s |
| coalescing window | 1.0 s | our apply transaction | 0.2 s |
| queue wait at 11% utilisation | 0.1 s | | |
| Salesforce write (A13, **not ours**) | 2.0 s | | |
| **total** | **4.1 s** | **total** | **5.7 s** |

**No inbound queue** — at A1's peak the endpoint commits 14 transactions a
second.

## 3. The subproblems, in the order I would build them

**Ordered by risk:** (1) getting it wrong loses data unrecoverably, (2) getting
it wrong is silent, (3) other code is built on the decision. That puts the merge
rule first and the backfill last — the opposite of the data's flow.

| | Subproblem | Why here | Demo |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **S1** | decide a field's current value, and keep what it displaced | all three: a wrong merge loses a real edit permanently and silently, and every write path is built on its schema | **yes** |
| **S2** | stop a change going round forever | the only self-amplifying failure — a loop eats the whole cap and stops sync for every record | **yes** |
| **S3** | hold outbound work on disk and spend the cap | S1's severity at lower likelihood; a transactional outbox is a known shape | **yes** |
| **S4** | make inbound delivery safe to repeat and to reorder | cannot be earlier ("older" needs S1's key); severe but detectable and replayable | **yes** |
| **S5** | know which record is which across the systems | a lost create response can duplicate a record: bad, but bounded and visible at once | no |
| **S6** | recover what was missed while a side was dark | **first to ask about**, sixth to build: fixed by re-running, but rests on A4 | no |
| **S7** | prove the webhook came from Salesforce | a gate, not a risk; stubbed day one, filled before production | no |
| **S8** | load the 5 million existing records | one-off, offline, no latency target, re-runnable | no |

**The demo exercises S1–S4 and nothing below** — exactly the four whose failures
are unrecoverable or silent: phone-and-city with full history (S1), our own
update returning and not being sent back (S2), a pending call surviving a restart
with Salesforce down and then draining under an enforced cap (S3), a duplicate
and an older event after a newer one (S4). S2, S6, S7 and S8 add **no process**.
