Review the whole branch against `main` (use `git diff main...HEAD --stat` to scope; the branch is the entire deliverable, ~30 commits).

CONTEXT — what this is. A take-home exercise deliverable: a design document plus an optional TypeScript demo for two-way sync of customer/contact records between Salesforce and a Postgres-backed portal. Deliverables are (1) `docs/design.md` following the exercise's 12-part outline, (2) the optional code: TypeScript on Node 20+, runs on Node alone against a fake Salesforce, `npm install` then `npm run demo`.

THE ASK I need you to check against, in priority order:

1. **Rule-for-rule consistency between code and design.** This is the most important axis. The exercise requires the code to match the design document rule for rule. `docs/design.md` states the rules (parts 5-10); `docs/design-appendix.md` holds the justification. Source docstrings cite design section numbers ("design 7.3", "design 8.3", "Appendix C.2", etc.). Check: does the code actually implement what the cited section says? Are any cited section numbers now dangling (the design doc was just heavily compressed and resectioned — 9.1-9.4 are now blockquote labels "**9.1 — L1, ...**")? Flag any place where code behaviour and the stated rule diverge.

2. **The four checks the exercise names must be demonstrated** by `npm run demo`: a duplicate webhook; an older event arriving after a newer one; our own update coming back as a webhook and NOT being sent to Salesforce again; a pending outbound call that survives a process restart while the fake Salesforce is down, then drains. #!/usr/bin/env bash
# Ensure a project worktree follows the agent-memory file convention.
# AGENTS.md is the real project-intrinsic knowledge file; CLAUDE.md is a
# real regular file whose canonical content is the two-line @AGENTS.md pointer
# that Claude Code inlines at load time. Creates a minimal AGENTS.md skeleton
# when neither file exists, promotes a real CLAUDE.md file when it is the only
# file present (unless it is already the canonical pointer), converts a correct
# CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md symlink into the pointer file, and refuses to clobber
# distinct real files or wrong symlinks.
# Owns the canonical "## Maintaining this file" self-governance wording for
# project AGENTS.md files, injecting it idempotently into created skeletons,
# promoted CLAUDE.md files, and existing AGENTS.md files lacking both the exact
# heading and the project-owned mark below (exact first line, LF or CRLF):
# <!-- firstmate:maintained-by-project -->
# Projects may place this mark at the start of the file and retain equivalent
# maintenance guidance under their own heading. It declares guidance is present, not
# permission to remove governance. No prose equivalence is inferred.
# Owns the canonical CLAUDE.md pointer content (the exact two-line @AGENTS.md
# form). A real-file pointer cannot follow a write into AGENTS.md, which is why
# the installer never creates a CLAUDE.md symlink.
# Refuses a case-variant real memory file such as a lowercase agents.md, so the
# pointer's @AGENTS.md import resolves to a real AGENTS.md on a case-sensitive
# filesystem (issue #389). The real-file pointer also eliminates the old
# uppercase-literal-target dangling-symlink hazard that a CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md
# link would have carried for that same mismatch.
# This is a worktree utility for crewmates, not a supervision script, so it does
# not call fm-guard.sh.
# Usage: fm-ensure-agents-md.sh [repo-or-worktree-dir]
set -eu

usage() {
  echo "usage: fm-ensure-agents-md.sh [repo-or-worktree-dir]" >&2
  cat >&2 <<'EOF'

To retain equivalent project-owned maintenance guidance without adding the
canonical section, use this exact first line of AGENTS.md (LF or CRLF):
<!-- firstmate:maintained-by-project -->
The mark declares retained guidance, not permission to remove governance.
Without the first-line mark or exact canonical heading, the helper adds the section.
EOF
}

case "${1:-}" in
  -h|--help)
    usage
    exit 0
    ;;
esac
[ "$#" -le 1 ] || { usage; exit 1; }

DIR=${1:-.}
[ -d "$DIR" ] || { echo "error: not a directory: $DIR" >&2; exit 1; }
DIR=$(cd "$DIR" && pwd -P)
cd "$DIR"

AGENTS=AGENTS.md
CLAUDE=CLAUDE.md

write_maintenance_section() {
  cat <<'EOF'

content.content:
## 5. The inbound path

**One HTTP request becomes one Postgres transaction**, with no network call
inside it and no background step. Appendix C.3 has the sequence: validate, claim
the `eventId`, lock the record, then four steps per field, then commit and 200.

- **(a) learn** records what Salesforce holds regardless of what (c) decides,
  which is what collapses repair into the single condition 8.3.
- **(b) restatement** skips a field restating the `sf_value` we already held (8.4).
- **(c) decide** takes the first case that applies — echo, value-already-equal
  (`confirmed`), the order-key comparison, `superseded` — and only here can a
  current value change.
- **(d) repair** is condition 8.3, after every field whatever happened to it.

**The duplicate claim and the apply share one transaction:** split them and a
crash between marks an event processed that was never applied, which Salesforce
will never resend. **Fields are independent**, so one event may apply `phone` and
supersede `city`, making the event's outcome `partial`.

> A change whose canonical value already equals the current value changes
> **nothing** — not the value, not the order key, and not history.

| Resolving the record | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** known `sf_id` | one indexed lookup, lock, proceed |
| **(b)** unknown `sf_id`, human `changedBy` | mint a `portal_id`, insert link and empty row, apply every field as a first write. **Recovery (10.3) reuses this** |
| **(c)** unknown `sf_id`, integration user | the echo of a create *we* made. **503 + `Retry-After: 5`, apply nothing**; by redelivery it is case (a). After 60 s, log loudly and treat as (b) |

**400 versus 500**, since a 400 discards the event forever: an unknown *field
name* earns one; a *value* we failed to canonicalise is our bug and earns a 500.

## 6. The outbound path
#################### PART 9
## 9. The rule that stops a loop

Ranked second of eight: a loop consumes the whole 100 req/s budget and stops sync
for every record at once, within seconds of deployment.

> **9.1 — L1, the structural rule.** Outbound work is created exactly when
> `field_version.sf_value` differs from a field's current value — condition 8.3,
> after every field, on both paths, and nowhere else.

```
portal sets city = Noida  -> sf_value "Gurugram" <> "Noida"  -> 1 outbound row
we PATCH Noida, 2xx       -> sf_value := "Noida"                            (6.3)
Salesforce echoes Noida   -> sf_value "Noida" = current       -> 0 rows.  Dead.
```

No fuel after one hop, because there is nothing left to disagree about.
**Precondition: canonical form (7.3).**

> **9.2 — L2, the actor rule.** A webhook whose `changedBy` is the integration user
> (A6) is an echo: recorded, never compared, never applied.

L1 guarantees the loop stops; L2 that it stops on the **right value**, since an
echo carries a later time than the edit our write overwrote and would otherwise
launder a stale value over a newer one (Appendix B).

> **9.3 — L3, the echo fence.** After a 2xx the sender records the record, field and
> hash of the canonical value sent, expiring in 15 minutes; an inbound change
> matching an unexpired entry is an echo.

> **9.4 — L4, the repair breaker.** Above **5 repairs to one field in an hour**,
> enqueue nothing more for it, mark it contested, and alert.

L3 is L2's guarantee keyed on the value rather than the actor, so it holds if A6
is false. L4 bounds the one way L1 fails: a spelling our canonical form does not
normalise makes every echo read as disagreement.

| | Guarantees | Absent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **L1** + canonical form | the loop **terminates** | everything; no other layer saves us |
| **L2** | it terminates on the **right value** | our own write launders a stale value over a newer one |
| L3 | L2's guarantee without A6 | nothing, while A6 holds |
| L4 | bounds L1's one failure mode | an unbounded argument over one field |

## 10. The 6-hour outage

+ * The merge itself is tested in `src/domain/merge.test.ts`. What is tested here
+ * is the part of design 5 that lives *outside* the merge: claiming the event,
+ * resolving which record a webhook is about, classifying our own echo, and the
+ * status code each refusal earns. Those are rule seams too — the three resolve
+ * cases and the L2/L3 echo classification are all stated rules — and a bug in
+ * them is invisible to the merge tests.
+import assert from "node:assert/strict";
+import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
+import { mkdtempSync, rmSync } from "node:fs";
+import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
+import { join } from "node:path";
+import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, test } from "node:test";
+import { INTEGRATION_USER } from "../salesforce/client.js";
+import { DurableStore } from "../store/store.js";
+import { ECHO_FENCE_TTL_MS, receiveWebhook } from "./endpoint.js";
+let dir: string;
+let store: DurableStore;
+beforeEach(() => {
+  dir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "sync-endpoint-"));
+  store = DurableStore.open(join(dir, "store.json"));
+afterEach(() => {
+  rmSync(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
+/** A webhook body in the shape the exercise's sample uses. */
+function body(over: Partial<Record<string, unknown>> = {}): string {
+  return JSON.stringify({
+    eventId: "evt_1",
+    objectType: "Contact",
+    occurredAt: 1_000,
+    changedBy: "sales.user@client.example",
+    changedFields: { city: "Gurugram" },
+    ...over,
+/** Deliver with a controllable clock, so the 60-second bound can be reached. */
+function deliverAt(nowMs: number, raw: string) {
+  return receiveWebhook(store, raw, () => nowMs);
+describe("receiveWebhook: the duplicate rule (design 8.1)", () => {
+  test("a byte-identical redelivery is a counted duplicate, not an error", () => {
+    const first = deliverAt(10_000, body());
+    const second = deliverAt(10_001, body());
+    assert.equal(first.status, 200);
+    assert.equal(second.status, 200);
+    assert.equal(second.body.status, "duplicate");
+    // Counted, not alerted: Salesforce did what A7 permits.
+    assert.equal(second.body.reason, undefined);
+  test("the same eventId with a different payload is reported as the provider bug it is", () => {
+    deliverAt(10_000, body());
+    const conflicting = deliverAt(10_001, body({ changedFields: { city: "Noida" } }));
+    // First write wins, and this one is distinguishable from an ordinary
+    // duplicate — the design contrasts the two deliberately (design 8.1).
+    assert.equal(conflicting.status, 200);
+    assert.equal(conflicting.body.reason, "eventId-reused-with-different-payload");
+    const values = store.read((tx) => tx.getRecord("Contact", resolvePortalId()));
+    assert.equal(values?.values.city, "Gurugram");
+describe("receiveWebhook: resolving the record (design 5 cases (a), (b), (c))", () => {
+  test("case (b): an unseen Salesforce record is minted and every field applied", () => {
+    const res = deliverAt(10_000, body());
+    assert.equal(res.status, 200);
+    assert.equal(res.body.status, "applied");
+    const record = store.read((tx) => tx.getRecord("Contact", resolvePortalId()));
+    assert.equal(record?.values.city, "Gurugram");
+  test("case (c): a create echo arriving before we recorded the id defers with a 503", () => {
+    // A portal-created record whose Salesforce id we do not have yet.
+    store.transaction((tx) => tx.createRecord("Contact", "portal-1", null));
+    const res = deliverAt(10_000, body({ changedBy: INTEGRATION_USER }));
+    assert.equal(res.status, 503);
+    assert.equal(res.body.reason, "create-echo-before-link");
+    // Applied nothing: by the redelivery the link exists and it is case (a).
+    assert.equal(store.read((tx) => tx.getRecord("Contact", "portal-1"))?.values.city, undefined);
+  test("case (c) is bounded: past 60 seconds it stops deferring and falls through to (b)", () => {
+    // The regression this pins: the bound used to read `linkedAtMs`, which is
+    // unset for exactly these unlinked rows, so the wait computed as 0 forever
+    // and a create that never linked refused every later webhook of its type
+    // with a permanent 503 (design 5 case (c) promises a 60-second bound).
+    store.transaction((tx) => tx.createRecord("Contact", "portal-1", null));
+    const deferred = deliverAt(10_000 + 59_000, body({ changedBy: INTEGRATION_USER }));
+    assert.equal(deferred.status, 503, "still inside the bound");
+    const fellThrough = deliverAt(
+      body({ eventId: "evt_2", changedBy: INTEGRATION_USER }),
+    assert.equal(fellThrough.status, 200, "past the bound, treated as case (b)");
+    assert.equal(fellThrough.body.status, "applied");
+describe("receiveWebhook: our own write coming back (design 9.2, 9.3)", () => {
+  test("L2: a webhook from the integration user is recorded, never applied", () => {
+    // Link the record first, so this is an echo rather than case (c).
+    store.transaction((tx) => {
+      tx.createRecord("Contact", "portal-1", "0031A00000001");
+      tx.setCurrentValue("Contact", "portal-1", "city", "Noida");
+    const res = deliverAt(10_000, body({ changedBy: INTEGRATION_USER }));
+    assert.equal(res.status, 200);
+    assert.equal(res.body.status, "echo");
+    // Never applied: the value we hold is untouched by Salesforce's echo.
+    assert.equal(store.read((tx) => tx.getRecord("Contact", "portal-1"))?.values.city, "Noida");
+  test("L3: an unexpired fence classifies an echo even when the actor does not (A6 false)", () => {
+    store.transaction((tx) => {
+      tx.createRecord("Contact", "portal-1", "0031A00000001");
+      tx.setCurrentValue("Contact", "portal-1", "city", "Gurugram");
+      tx.addEchoFence({
+        objectType: "Contact",
+        portalId: "portal-1",
+        field: "city",
+        valueHash: sha256OfGurugram(),
+        sentAtMs: 9_000,
+        expiresAtMs: 9_000 + ECHO_FENCE_TTL_MS,
+    // A human actor, so L2 does not fire; the fence is what recognises it.
+    const res = deliverAt(10_000, body({ changedBy: "someone.else@client.example" }));
+    assert.equal(res.body.status, "echo");
+describe("receiveWebhook: the event's own outcome (design 5)", () => {
+  test("an event whose every field already holds the incoming value is confirmed, not applied", () => {
+    store.transaction((tx) => {
+      tx.createRecord("Contact", "portal-1", "0031A00000001");
+      tx.setCurrentValue("Contact", "portal-1", "city", "Gurugram");
+    const res = deliverAt(10_000, body());
+    // Nothing changed, so the event must not read as one that changed
+    // something — the same reason design 5 keeps it out of `field_change`.
+    assert.equal(res.body.status, "confirmed");
+  test("an unknown field name earns a 400, which discards the event forever", () => {
+    const res = deliverAt(10_000, body({ changedFields: { telephon: "x" } }));
+    assert.equal(res.status, 400);
+/** The portal id minted for the sample record, whatever it was. */
+function resolvePortalId(): string {
+  const link = store.read((tx) => tx.findLinkBySfId("Contact", "0031A00000001"));
+  assert.ok(link, "the webhook should have minted a link");
+  return link.portalId;
+/** The canonical hash of "Gurugram", as the sender would have recorded it. */
+function sha256OfGurugram(): string {
+  // Imported lazily to keep this helper beside its one use.
+  return createHash("sha256").update("Gurugram").digest("hex");

=== C.3 step (c) ===
  |            A null sf_value means we have never heard Salesforce's value
  |            for this field, so the incoming value is a change, not a
  |            restatement. This runs in both payload shapes -- see 8.4.
  |
  |        (c) decide the current value:
  |            if echo:                                                     (part 9)
  |                sync_observation('echo')          -- no value change, ever
  |            else if order_key(incoming) > order_key(stored):             (7.2)
  |                UPDATE customer/contact SET <field> = value
  |                UPSERT field_version with the new stamp
  |                INSERT field_change(outcome='applied', old_value, new_value)
  |            else if value is distinct from the current value:
  |                INSERT field_change(outcome='superseded')                (part 8.2)
  |            else:
  |                sync_observation('confirmed')
  |
  |        (d) the one repair condition, checked after every field:         (8.3)
  |            if field_version.sf_value is distinct from the current value:
  |                INSERT outbound_change(reason='repair')
  |
  |-- 8. UPDATE inbound_event SET outcome = <applied|echo|superseded|partial>
=== DDL CHECKs ===
CREATE TABLE sync_observation (
  object_type text, portal_id uuid, field text,
  observed_value text, occurred_at timestamptz(3),
  origin text, origin_event_id text, actor text,
  outcome text NOT NULL CHECK (outcome IN ('echo','confirmed')),
  observed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp()
) PARTITION BY RANGE (observed_at);         -- monthly partitions, dropped at 90 days

-- inbound idempotency. Part 8.1.
CREATE TABLE inbound_event (
  event_id     text PRIMARY KEY,              -- Salesforce's eventId
  object_type  text NOT NULL,
  sf_id        text NOT NULL,
  occurred_at  timestamptz(3) NOT NULL,
  payload_hash bytea NOT NULL,                -- sha256 of the raw body
  outcome      text NOT NULL,                 -- applied | echo | superseded | partial | rejected
  received_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp()
);
CREATE INDEX ON inbound_event (received_at);  -- for the 30-day prune
=== E table ===
| **`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`** (the per-record lock) | nothing: one process, one transaction at a time | **imitated.** The demo cannot show that the lock serialises competing merges, because it has no concurrency |
| **`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`** | the `leaseOwner` / `leaseUntilMs` columns the design already carries | **yes** — the lease, and its reclaim after a sender dies, are real |
| **the partial unique index** (one pending row per field) | an explicit check in the enqueue path | imitated |
| **`LISTEN` / `NOTIFY`** | the demo calls the worker directly | imitated |
| **monthly partitions and pruning** | not implemented | absent — retention is a design concern, not a rule |
| **the live Salesforce record API** | a fake written for this repository, file-backed so it survives the restart, with levers for the four behaviours the rules depend on: it echoes every write, it can be unreachable, it can answer 429, and it can refuse a record's data | the second adapter at the seam (part 2) |
| **HTTPS to the webhook endpoint** | the handler is called in-process, with the signature still verified over the raw body | imitated — the rules live in the handler, not in the HTTP framing |

git add src/ && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Fix four rules the code got wrong, and test the endpoint that hid them

A self-review against the design found the inbound endpoint had no test file,
and that is where three of these were hiding.

Design 5 case (c) promised a 60-second bound on deferring a create echo, and
the bound was unreachable: it read `linkedAtMs`, which is set only when an
`sfId` is attached and so is always unset for exactly the unlinked rows the
bound applies to. The subtraction was therefore always zero, and because the
branch matches ANY unlinked record of that object type, a portal create that
never linked would refuse every later webhook of its type with a 503 forever.
The link row now carries its own `createdAtMs` - the age of the row is what the
rule meant - and a test walks the clock past 60 s.

Design 8.1 says a repeated eventId carrying a different payload is the one
duplicate case that IS alerted, in contrast to the ordinary one. The comment
said so and no alert was raised; it now warns like the three comparable sites.

Design 6.5's settle table has a 401/403 row whose consequence is "stop the
sender": a credential failure was landing in the unexpected-error fallback,
counting toward the circuit breaker and letting every remaining row spend an
attempt on a call that could not succeed. Added SalesforceAuthFailed, the
branch that keeps the work and stops, and the fake lever that exercises it.

A store failure was reported as an endpoint failure: `tx.linkSfId` sat inside
the send's try-block, so a disk problem incremented the breaker counter and
told the caller Salesforce was at fault. Only the call is in the try now; the
store write follows it and propagates, which the conventions require, and the
lease expiry is what retries - safe because the upsert is idempotent on our own
portalId.

Also honest-outcome fixes the review surfaced: an event whose every field
already held the incoming value recorded `applied`, which is the rounding
design 5 argues against, so EventOutcome gained `confirmed`; the nothing-owed
skip wrote a success note into `lastError`; the hex check in validate.ts was
unreachable, because Buffer.from drops invalid bytes rather than throwing, so
it is now an explicit test; and store.transaction's catch-and-rethrow said it
performed the rollback when going out of scope is what does.

12 new tests, 113 -> 125. The demo's six scenarios stay green.
EOF
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Correct the design where the code was right and the document was not

Rule-for-rule means the document is wrong when they disagree, not just the code.

Appendix C.3's build sequence still had step (c) as echo -> order key ->
superseded -> confirmed, while the body, F.5 and the code take value-equality
BEFORE the order-key comparison. Those are not the same rule: a change matching
the value we hold but carrying a newer stamp would be `applied` under C.3 and
would restamp the field, which is the ownership theft F.5 exists to forbid. A
teammate building from C.3 would have implemented it. Fixed, with the ordering
called out so it cannot be flattened again.

The published DDL would have rejected rows the code writes: sync_observation's
CHECK allowed only echo and confirmed, so the first full-record restatement -
design 8.4's own traced hazard - would raise a constraint violation. The
inbound_event outcome vocabulary was short two values for the same reason.

Numbers the body states and the code did not: 6.4's decrease hard-coded a floor
of 5 that appears nowhere in the code, so it is now the parameter it always was
with the demo's floor recorded in Appendix E beside the cap and the lease. 9.4's
"above 5 repairs" was readable two ways, and the tests pin the boundary
deliberately, so the rule now says which side it falls on.

10.3 lost its claim-time skip to the compression, leaving that code path with no
stated rule at all; restored. And the subsection renumbering left seven stale
pointers inside the appendix (6.6, 6.7, three 6.5s, a 6.4, and a "5.1 case (b)"
from when part 5 had subsections), plus Appendix F starting at F.2 without
saying why.
EOF

Done — ready on `fm/tequity-sync-r1`, 39 commits, clean fast-forward onto `main`, nothing pushed.

## What the review turned up, and what I did

The self-review found real bugs, and the most important one was a rule the design promised and the code could not deliver:

- **Design 5's 60-second bound on deferring a create echo was unreachable.** It measured from `linkedAtMs`, which is set *only* when a Salesforce id is attached — so it is always unset for exactly the unlinked rows the bound applies to. The subtraction was always zero. Because the branch matches *any* unlinked record of that object type, a portal create that never linked would have refused every later webhook of its type with a permanent 503. The link row now carries its own `createdAtMs`, and a test walks the clock past 60 s.
- **A store failure was reported as an endpoint failure.** `tx.linkSfId` sat inside the send's try-block, so a disk problem incremented the circuit-breaker counter and told the caller Salesforce was at fault. Only the call is in the try now.
- **Design 8.1's one alerted duplicate case wasn't alerted** — the comment said it was.
- **Design 6.5's 401/403 row wasn't implemented**, so a credential failure fell into the generic fallback and every remaining row would have spent an attempt on a call that could not succeed. Added the error type, the stop, and a fake lever that exercises it.

On the design side, rule-for-rule cuts both ways, so where the code was right I fixed the document: **Appendix C.3's build sequence still stated the pre-value-equality branch order** — a teammate building from it would have restamped order keys on no-op re-saves, the exact ownership theft F.5 forbids. The published DDL also would have rejected `restatement` rows the code writes, which is design 8.4's own traced hazard. And my compression had left seven stale subsection pointers and dropped 10.3's claim-time skip rule entirely.

**Tests: 113 → 126**, including a new `endpoint.test.ts` — that file had no tests, which is precisely where three of the four code bugs were hiding. Demo: 6 scenarios, all green from a fresh clone with no `dist/` or state.

## What I did not change

Two findings I judged were the prose, not the behaviour: "above 5 repairs" reads two ways and the tests pin that boundary deliberately, so I made the rule say which side it falls on rather than shift a threshold. I also left the duplicated observation literals in `merge.ts` and the `(objectType, portalId, field)` data clump alone — both are real improvements, neither is worth refactoring the most sensitive module for on delivery day.

## One thing to decide, captain

The design document is **5,933 words, ~12 pages — not the 4–6 you asked for.** I measured the floor honestly: the 12-part outline, the 16-assumption table, the eight risk-ordered subproblems, the rule tables and the arithmetic come to ~5,800 words before a single sentence of connective prose. Every rule, number and required enumeration is intact and all justification moved to `design-appendix.md`, which is the substance of your point 1 — but the page count isn't met, and getting there means deleting things the exercise's own outline asks for. That call is yours; the commit message states the trade-off rather than hiding it.

The exercise is due 10:00 IST today, so if you want the document cut further, that's the one task left worth doing before submission.
